Understanding the mechanisms behind micro-aeration to enhance 
anaerobic digestion of corn straw 
Rong Zhu a,d, Dong-Hui Wang a, Yi Zheng d, Hua Zou a,c,*, Shan-Fei Fu a,b,c 
a Jiangsu Key Laboratory of Anaerobic Biotechnology, School of Environment and Civil Engineering, Jiangnan University, NO.1800 Lihu Avenue, Wuxi, Jiangsu Province 
214122, PR China 
b Shandong Industrial Engineering Laboratory of Biogas Production & Utilization, Key Laboratory of Biofuels, Shandong Provincial Key Laboratory of Synthetic Biology, 
Qingdao Institute of Bioenergy and Bioprocess Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, NO. 189 Songling Road, Qingdao 266101, PR China 
c Jiangsu Collaborative Innovation Center of Technology and Material of Water Treatment, Suzhou University of Science and Technology, Suzhou 215009, PR China 
d Department of Grain Science and Industry, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506, United States   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Anaerobic digestion 
Corn straw 
Micro-aeration 
Soluble humic acid 
Microbial community 
A B S T R A C T   
Micro-aeration has been shown to be favorable for anaerobic digestion (AD) process. However, the underlying 
mechanisms are not fully revealed. In this study, the effects of micro-aeration on AD process were investigated, 
the underlying mechanisms were also explored by comprehensively analysis of the substrate degradation, in­
termediate products, electron-transfer capacity, key enzymes and microbial communities. Results showed micro- 
aeration could benefit the AD process, and the beneficial effects were oxygen intensity-dependent. Maximum 
methane yield (262.0 ± 6.0 mL/(g⋅VS)) was achieved at micro-aeration of 0.2 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day), which was 7.8% 
higher than that of the control (without micro-aeration). The volatile fatty acids concentration, cellulase activity, 
soluble humic acids (SHAs) concentration and substrate degradation rate were all enhanced under micro- 
aeration condition. Moreover, micro-aeration could regulate the bacterial and archaeal communities: bacterial 
diversities and relative abundances of facultative and acetate-oxidizing bacteria (e.g., Firmicutes, Synergistota and 
Spirochaetota) increased, leading to higher substrate utilization rate; archaeal diversities decreased while oxygen- 
tolerating methanogens (e.g., Methanobacterium) became dominant to promote the methanogenesis. AD system 
with micro-aeration showed higher electron-transfer capacity and better conductive environment due to the 
increased SHAs concentration. The increased relative abundance of direct-interspecies-electron-transfer (DIET)- 
associated microbes could be favorable to DIET-based syntrophic methanogenesis which promotes AD under 
micro-aeration.   
1. Introduction 
Lignocellulosic biomass, such as agricultural and forest residues, 
energy crops, and grasses is the most abundant renewable bioresource 
on the Earth [1]. Corn is one of the most important grain crops in China, 
and the yearly yield of corn crop is estimated to be 520 million tons, 
which yields 260 million tons of corn straw as a major by-product [2,3]. 
Corn straw has been proved to be a potential substrate for biogas pro­
duction via anaerobic digestion (AD). Many biogas plants that use corn 
straw as feedstock are built every year in China. Although promising, 
some barriers still exist in AD of corn straw, among which the low hy­
drolysis efficiency caused by the recalcitrant structure of corn straw is 
generally regarded as the rate-limiting step [4]. 
In order to enhance the AD efficiency of corn straw, various substrate 
pretreatment methods have been extensively studied, including phys­
ical, chemical and biological pretreatments as well as their combinations 
[5–8]. However, these pretreatment methods have their respective 
inherent shortcomings, e.g., need of chemicals, high energy consump­
tion and/or long residence time. Another choice to improve the AD ef­
ficiency of cellulosic substrate is to manage or alter the microbial 
community composition through bioaugmentation, enrichment and/or 
stimulation of specific indigenous microorganisms [9]. Micro-aeration 
by introducing limited amount of oxygen into the AD system has been 
proved to be a potential strategy to address the challenge of low hy­
drolysis efficiency associated with AD of cellulosic substrate [10,11]. As 
reported, micro-aeration during AD can stimulate the growth of facul­
tative anaerobes which excrete more extracellular enzymes to improve 
hydrolysis and fermentation of lignocellulosic biomass, thus enhancing

the AD efficiency [12–14]. Given its potential economic and environ­
mental benefits, micro-aeration during AD has received increasing 
attention. However, no consistent even contradictory conclusions have 
been made about the effect of micro-aeration on the AD process. Some 
researchers reported that micro-aeration increased the hydrolysis effi­
ciency, VFAs (volatile fatty acids) formation and methane yield during 
AD [15–17], while others found no even negative effect of micro- 
aeration on the AD process [18–20]. Such a conflict could be because 
the underlying mechanisms of micro-aeration remain unclear. Further­
more, the responses of bacteria and archaea, the enzyme activities and 
the degradation characteristics of different components (e.g., cellulose, 
hemicellulose and lignin) under micro-aeration conditions were rarely 
reported. 
Therefore, this work aimed to investigate the effects of micro- 
aeration on AD of corn straw. In addition, the underlying mechanisms 
of how micro-aeration benefit the AD process were explored using 
comprehensive analytic methods include intermediate products anal­
ysis, model-based analysis, microbial community structure analysis, 
cyclic voltammetry (CV) and conductivity tests. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Substrate and inoculum 
Corn straw was collected from a corn farm in Xuzhou, Jiangsu 
Province, China and used as a substrate in this study. The corn straw was 
air-dried to the moisture content of 6.6 ± 0.2%, and ground to 0.5-cm 
particles before used. The inoculum used in this study was obtained 
from an AD reactor which uses corn straw as a substrate and is operated 
at 37 ◦C. Before used, the inoculum was filtered through a 10-mesh sieve 
to remove large particles (e.g., undigested corn straw). The character­
istics of substrate and inoculum were shown in Table 1. 
2.2. Batch biomethane potential (BMP) test 
The batch mesophilic (37 ◦C) AD of corn straw was carried out in 
triplicate with a total fermentation time of 40 days. Before AD, 5.6 g (TS) 
corn straw and 2.0 g (TS) inoculum were mixed in 300-mL glass bottles. 
The biogas production with the inoculum only (i.e., no corn straw) was 
also carried out as a blank group. The working volume was adjusted to 
200 mL by adding nutrient solution as described by Angelidaki et al 
[21]. All the bottles were then purged with argon for 5 min to remove 
the air and sealed with rubber stoppers. All the bottles were incubated in 
a shaking air bath at 37 ◦C with the shaking speed of 200 rpm. In order to 
create different micro-aeration intensity, oxygen of different doses was 
injected into the bottles daily by using a syringe. The tested oxygen 
doses included 0 (control), 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mL/ 
(g⋅VS⋅day), which were denoted by MA0, MA0.05, MA0.1, MA0.2, 
MA0.4, MA0.8 and MA1.6, respectively. 
2.3. Model-based analysis 
The modified Gompertz model (Eq. (1)) [22] was adapted to fit the 
methane production data for analyzing the effects of micro-aeration on 
AD of corn straw.

2.4. Microbial community structure analysis 
When the operation of AD systems became stable (i.e., the 13th day 
of AD in current study), 10 mL of digestate were collected from three 
representative AD groups such as MA0 (control without micro-aeration), 
MA0.2 (positive effect of micro-aeration) and MA1.6 (overdose of micro- 
aeration) for microbial community structure analysis. The microbial 
community structure was analyzed by the Majorbio Bio-Pharm Tech­
nology (Shanghai, China) using the high throughput sequencing 
method. According to the instructions, the E.Z.N.A.® DNA Kit (Omega 
Biotek, Norcross, GA, USA) was used to extract the DNA from the 
digestates. In order to run the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), a primer 
set of 338F (ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG) and 806R (GGAC­
TACHVGGGTWTCTAAT) was used to amplify the V3-V4 region of the 
bacterial 16S rRNA gene, and a primer set of 524F (TGY­
CAGCCGCCGCGGTAA) and 958R (YCCGGCGTTGAVTCCAATT) was 
used to amplify the V4-V5 region of the archaeal 16S rRNA gene [23]. 
The quantification of the PCR products was performed with the Quan­
tiFluor™-ST blue fluorescence quantitative system (Promega Inc., 
China). The Illumina MiSeq platform was used to pool the obtained 
amplicons from the PCR reactions in equimolar and paired-end 
sequenced. 
The QIIME package was used to extract the high-quality sequences 
(Quantitative Insights Into Microbial Ecology) (V1.9.1). Raw data were 
first checked for barcode and adapter integrity, and the low-quality se­
quences that contained ambiguity and less than 200 basis points were 
deleted to obtain effective sequencing data. The operational taxonomic 
unit (OTU) for the sequence set was classified by RDP Classifier (Ribo­
somalDatabase Project) (V2.11) with the consistency threshold of 97% 
identity. The identification and removal of chimeric sequences were 
done by using Usearch (V7.1), and the classification of SILVA132 16S 
rRNA database was done by using RDP Classifier with the confidence 
threshold of 80%. 
2.5. Analytical methods 
2.5.1. Excitation emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence spectra for digestate 
analysis 
EEM fluorescence spectra was applied to characterize dissolved 
organic matter in the digestates to study the effect of oxygen dose on the 
dissolved organic matter. After 40 days of fermentation, 1 mL digestate 
was filtered through 0.45-μm filters and diluted 5x using deionized 
water before the EEM measurement by a fluorescence spectrophotom­
eter (F-7000 FL, HitachiCo, Japan). The excitation wavelength was 
gradually increased from 200 to 450 nm while emission wavelength was 
gradually increased from 250 to 650 nm by a 5-nm increment. The three- 
dimensional fluorescence region formed by the excitation and emission 
wavelengths was used to divide the organics in each digestate into five 
groups as shown in Table 2. 
2.5.2. Analysis of soluble humic acids (SHAs) in the digestate 
According to the polyphenol theory of humus formation, lignin, 
cellulose and other non-lignin substances can be converted to humic 
acids (HAs) or fulvic acids by microbes in AD process (Fig. S1) [25]. 
Thus, high concentration of HAs or fulvic acids in the digestates could 
indicate high degradation of corn straw. Moreover, SHAs were also

reported to serve as electron transport media and benefit the direct

duction [24,26]. SHAs in the digestate were extracted according to the 
procedure developed by the International Humic Substances Society 
(IHSS) [27]. Before the extraction of SHAs, 20 mL samples were 
centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 15 min and then filtered through 0.45-um 
filters. To the filtrates, 6 mol/L HCl was added to reduce the pH to 1.0 
for precipitating out HAs, and 6 mol/L NaOH was then used to dissolve 
the HAs precipitates. Such a procedure of precipitation-dissolution- 
precipitation was repeated for three times to purify the SHAs pre­
cipitates. The SHAs were quantified in g/L according to the gravimetric 
method [28]. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy of SHAs 
precipitates (freeze-drying) were conducted by using IRTracer-100, 
Shimadzu, Japan. 
2.5.3. Lignocellulosic compositions analysis of corn straw 
Extractives of corn straw were first removed by water and ethyl 
alcohol extraction for 24 h [29], and the residual extractive-free corn 
straw was used for the analysis of structural carbohydrates and lignin 
[30]. Briefly, the extractive–free corn straw underwent a two-step acid 
hydrolysis: 72% sulfuric acid (3.00 ± 0.01 mL) was first used to hy­
drolyze corn straw (300.0 ± 10 mg) in a water bath at 30 ◦C for 60 min, 
and then the acid was diluted to 4% by adding 84.00 ± 0.04 mL of 
deionized water and autoclaved for 60 min at 121 ◦C. The hydrolysate 
was vacuum-filtered through a filtering crucible. The acid insoluble 
lignin of corn straw was measured by weight difference before and after 
the ashing of the solid residue, and the acid soluble lignin in the filtrate 
was determined on a UV–Vis spectroscopy (P1, MAPADA Co, China) at 
320 nm. The monosaccharides in the filtrate were quantified by using a 
high pressure ion chromatography (DIONEX ICS-5000 + SP-5, Thermo 
Fisher Scientific, USA) equipped with CarboPac PA20 column (3-mm 
diameter × 150-mm length). The injection volume was 5 μL, and the 
mobile phase consisted of 1 mol/L sodium acetate and 250 mmol/L 
NaOH in HPLC grade water. 
2.5.4. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and conductivity test of digestate 
CV analysis could be performed to illustrate the redox property of 
special material and/or system [31]. The digestate samples from MA0, 
MA0.2 and MA1.6 were firstly centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 10 min, the 
supernatants were used for CV and conductivity test. The CV experiment 
was carried out to excavate the redox reactions in digestate with a three- 
electrode electrochemical cell in a single chamber [32]. The reference 
electrode, counter electrode and working electrode in the electro­
chemical cell were saturated calomel electrode (SCE, Huachen, China), 
Pt and carbon cloth (2*2 cm), respectively. Digestate of 140 mL was 
added into the electrochemical cell, and the cell was purged with N2 for 
5 min to remove the dissolved oxygen. CV was tested on an electro­
chemical workstation (CHI600E, Huachen, China) with a scanning 
voltage in the range of −1.0 ~ 1.0 V (versus SCE) at 50 mV/S scan rate. 
The electric conductivity shows the talent of electron transfer for spe­
cific material and/or system, which could their abilities in participation 
of DIET [33]. The conductivity of digestate was measured by using 
conductivity meter (DDS-307, Leici, China). 
2.5.5. Cellulase activity analysis 
The cellulase activity was determined by using DNS (dinitrosalicylic 
acid) method [34]. Samples were first centrifuged at 11,800 rpm for 15 
min at 4 ◦C, and the supernatants were collected and balanced at 37 ◦C 
for 10 min. The mixture of 1.00 mL of sodium carboxymethyl cellulose 
(CMC-Na), 2.00 mL of DNS, 0.50 mL of balanced sample, and 5 mL of 
deionized water was incubated in a water bath at 37 ◦C for 60 min. 
Afterwards, the mixture was heated in boiling water for 5 min to stop the 
enzymatic reaction and cooled down to ambient temperature. The 
mixture was then diluted to 25 mL, and the absorbance was read at 540 
nm on a UV–Visible spectrophotometer (P1, MAPADA Co, China). The 
calibration curve was made by using glucose as a standard with a series 
of concentrations. 
2.5.6. Other analyses 
The water displacement method was used to monitor the biogas 
production in volume, and the methane content of biogas was analyzed 
by using a gas chromatograph equipped with a thermal conductivity 
detector and a Porapak Q stainless steel analytical column (OD × L = 3 
mm × 180 cm) (SP 6890, Shandong Lunan Inc., China) [35]. The pH was 
determined using a compact pH-meter (LAQUAtwin-pH-33, Horiba Co., 
Japan). The TS and VS were determined according to the gravimetric 
method. To measure VFAs concentration, samples were first centrifuged 
at 5000 rpm for 15 min, and the supernatants were filtered through 
0.45-μm filters. After acidified with 3 M phosphoric acid, the VFAs 
concentration was analyzed on a gas chromatograph (GC-2010, Shi­
madzu, Japan). The total VFAs were determined by summing up each 
individual VFA (i.e., acetate, propionate, butyrate/isobutyrate, 
valerate/ isovalerate, caproate, heptanoate and caprylate). All analyses 
were conducted in triplicates unless specified, otherwise. The one-way 
ANOVA (analysis of variance) was performed to test the significance 
of difference between different treatments with Pcritical = 0.05 using SPSS 
software (ver. 16.0, IBM, USA). 
3. Results 
3.1. Methane production from anaerobic digestion of corn straw 
As shown in Fig. 1, the AD reactors treated by different micro- 
aeration intensities had similar trends in cumulative methane yield, 
while the amount of cumulative methane yield was significantly affected 
by the micro-aeration (p < 0.05). The highest 40-day cumulative 
methane yield of 262.0 ± 6.0 mL/(g⋅VS) was obtained with micro- 
aeration intensity of 0.2 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day) (MA0.2), which was 7.8%

higher than that of MA0. However, further increase of micro-aeration 
intensity impaired the methane yield compared to MA0. When micro- 
aeration intensity reached 1.6 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day) (MA1.6), the cumulative 
methane yield was only 215.9 ± 2.9 mL/(g⋅VS), which was 11.2% lower 
than that of MA0. In current study, the whole AD process was divided 
into three stages based on the fermentation time, including early AD 
stage (the 1st ~ 13th day), middle AD stage (the 14th ~ 26th day) and 
late AD stage (the 27th ~ 40th day) [36]. The cumulative methane 
yields of different AD stages were shown in Table 3. Compared to MA0, 
the methane production increased with the increase of micro-aeration 
intensity from 0.05 to 0.2 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day). In the early AD stage, the 
highest methane yield of 113.0 ± 2.4 mL/(g⋅VS) was obtained from 
MA0.2, which was 23.3% higher than that of MA0. Further increase of 
micro-aeration intensity reduced the methane yields, i.e., the methane 
yields of MA0.8 and MA1.6 are only 96% and 43% of MA0, respectively. 
In the middle AD stage, the methane yield of MA1.6 was 120.1 ± 2.7 
mL/(g⋅VS), which accounted for 55% of its total (40 days) methane yield 
and was 9%, 10%, 10%, 11%, 15% and 16% higher than that of MA0, 
MA0.05, MA0.1, MA0.2, MA0.4 and MA1.6, respectively. In the late AD 
stage, the highest methane production (56.0 ± 5.7 mL/g⋅VS) was still 
obtained by MA1.6, which was 35% higher than that of MA0. 
In order to further analyze the effect of micro-aeration on AD, the 
modified Gompertz was used to fit the experimental data of methane 
production. The fitting results are shown in Table 4. The experimental 
data were well fitted to the modified Gompertz model, and all the R2 
values are higher than 0.99. The micro-aeration intensity less than or 
equal to 0.2 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day) raised methane yield potential (Mm) and 
maximum methane production rate (Rm) but reduced lag phase time (λ). 
Further increase of micro-aeration intensity lowered the methane yield 
potential and the maximum methane production rate but increased the 
lag phase time. The micro-aeration also affected the time required to 
produce 80% of the total methane yield (T80), which increased with the 
increase of micro-aeration intensity from 0.05 to 1.6 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day), and 
the shortest T80 was obtained by MA0.05 (24.5 days), which was 2.3 
days shorter than that of MA0. 
3.2. Impact of micro-aeration on daily methane yield, cellulase activity 
and volatile fatty acids 
Three groups (MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6) were selected and compared 
to analyze the effects of micro-aeration on the AD process. As shown in 
Fig. 2, the daily methane yields of MA0 and MA0.2 had the same ten­
dency. There were two methane production peaks for MA0 and MA02 
and the maximum peak values were obtained at the 10th and 9th day of 
AD, respectively. However, the daily methane yield of MA1.6 only 
showed one methane production peak at the 15th day of AD, which 
might be caused by the inhibition of the methanogen activity under high 
micro-aeration intensity. 
The variations of cellulase activity and total VFA (TVFA) concen­
trations during AD of corn straw are demonstrated in Fig. 3. The cellu­
lase activity of these three groups showed the same tendencies: raised 
rapidly at the first 6 days and leveled off afterwards with slight fluctu­
ation until the end of AD (Fig. 3a). The cellulase activity of MA0, MA0.2 
and MA 1.6 showed no obvious difference during the first 6 days of AD. 
After that, the cellulase activity of MA0.2 and MA 1.6 reached the peak 
values at the 12th day, which were 15% and 20% higher than that of 
MA0, respectively. 
According to Fig. 3b, the TVFA concentrations under micro-aeration 
conditions (MA0.2 and MA1.6) were higher than that of MA0 after the 
3rd day of AD and stayed at high level for a longer period. The peak 
value of the TVFA concentration of MA0 was 2648 ± 75 mg/L at the 3rd 
day, while the TVFA peak concentrations of MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 
2368 ± 81 mg/L and 2396 ± 56 mg/L at the 6th and 9th day, respec­
tively. The delay of the TVFA peaks under micro-aeration might be due 
to the fact that oxygen promotes the growth of facultative bacteria that 
could consume part of VFAs [11]. However, the VFAs under micro- 
aeration condition remained much higher concentration for longer 
time. This could be explained by the fact that the facultative bacteria 
could excrete more extracellular cellulase to enhance the hydrolysis of 
corn straw, thus producing high VFAs concentrations (i.e., MA0.2 and 
MA1.6). Moreover, enzyme activity and VFAs were close but the 
methane yield differed between MA0.2 and MA1.6. The reason behind 
this phenomenon might be that methanogenesis was inhibited by excess 
oxygen and VFAs were consumed by facultative bacteria using oxygen as 
an electron acceptor in MA1.6.

MA1.6 were 1.31 ± 0.06 g/L, 1.67 ± 0.12 and 2.05 ± 0.10 g/L, 
respectively (Fig. 4d). These findings suggested that the addition of

SHAs concentration, which could benefit the DIET based syntrophic

intensively studied [24,37]. However, little research has been done on 
the generation of HAs from AD of corn straw, and the effects of HAs on 
the AD of lignocellulosic biomass need to be further explored. 
3.4. Cyclic voltammetry and conductivity of digestate 
Electrochemical methods can be used to characterize these redox 
reactions, therefore, CV experiment was conducted in this study to 
analyze the electron transfer capacity of the AD system [38]. Fig. 5a 
shows CVs of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6. It could be observed that three 
distinct redox peaks with potentials of 0.60 (peak1), 0.27 (peak2) and 
−0.24 V (peak3) (versus saturated calomel electrode) presented in all 
three groups at the scan rate of 50 mV/s, however, the peak currents of 
MA0.2 and MA1.6 were different. The peak1 currents of MA0.2 and 
MA1.6 were 24% and 38% higher than that of MA0, and the peak2 
currents of MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 75% and 96% higher than that of 
MA0, while peak3 currents showed no difference among three groups. 
The higher peak currents observed in digestate from MA0.2 and MA1.6 
demonstrated their higher capacity of electron transfer, which could 
attribute to the increased SHAs concentrations. FTIR analysis showed 
that freeze-dried SHAs possessed abundance of surface oxygen- 
containing functional groups (C–O, C––O and C–O; shown in 
Fig. S2), which could be used as electron shuttle to accept and donate 
electrons, leading to higher capacity of electron transfer [31]. Conduc­
tivity was crucial to triggering the direct interspecies electron transfer 
(DIET)-based syntrophic methane production in anaerobic digestion 
[39]. The conductivity values of digestate sampled from MA0, MA0.2 
and MA1.6 were 3,173 ± 52, 3,773 ± 43 and 4,290 ± 30 μs/cm, 
respectively (Fig. 5b). The results indicated that micro-aeration could 
create a better conductive environment for syntrophic microorganisms. 
3.5. Variation of structural compositions and component removal of corn 
straw during AD 
The structural compositions of raw corn straw and biogas residue of 
MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 are shown in Fig. 6a. The contents of cellulose, 
hemicellulose and lignin of substrate (raw corn straw) were 34.00 ±
2.01%, 19.45 ± 4.55% and 22.71% ± 0.71%, respectively. The chemi­
cal composition analysis of the biogas residues showed that the cellulose 
contents of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 decreased to 22.75 ± 2.75%, 
21.59% ± 0.59% and 21.59% ± 1.59%, respectively after AD. Similarly, 
the hemicellulose contents of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 decreased to 
10.30% ± 1.69%, 10.46% ± 0.53% and 9.46% ± 1.46%, respectively 
after AD. In contrast, the lignin contents of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 
increased to 33.83% ± 2.17%, 33.22% ± 1.22% and 33.26% ± 3.73%, 
respectively. The opposite variation of cellulose/hemicellulose and 
lignin might be caused by their respective chemical properties. Cellulose 
and hemicellulose were amenable to biodegradation, while lignin was 
recalcitrant to the AD process. Thus, the digestion time for cellulose and 
hemicellulose was much shorter than that of lignin, e.g., 14, 2 and 60 
days, respectively [40]. 
The cellulose removal rates of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 62.46% 
± 2.30%, 68.23%± 2.01% and 69.90% ± 3.12%, respectively, and the 
hemicellulose removal rates of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 70.28% ±
1.40%, 73.10% ± 2.01% and 76.95% ± 3.32%, respectively (Fig. 6b). 
However, the lignin removal rates of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 
much lower, reaching 16.48% ± 2.71%, 26.85% ± 1.20% and 30.58% 
± 2.17%, respectively. Such data could indicate that micro-aeration 
increased the degradation rates of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin 
to different extents, which was consistent with previous studies 
[10,11,41]. In addition, higher micro-aeration intensity led to higher 
cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin degradation, e.g., the cellulose, 
hemicellulose and lignin removal rates of MA1.6 are 12.05%, 9.53% and 
85.51% higher than those of MA0. The higher degradation of corn straw 
and lower methane yield in MA1.6 could be explained by the con­
sumption of available substrate by facultative bacteria using oxygen as 
an electron acceptor and the inhibition of methanogenesis by excess 
oxygen. 
3.6. Microbial community structure analysis 
The digestate samples from MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 used for the 
microbial community analysis were collected at the 13th day of AD. The 
Shannon diversity indexes of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 3.26, 3.78 
and 4.30, respectively, which reflected higher microbial diversities 
under micro-aeration condition (Fig. S4). Similarly, Lim et al. [42] and 
Fu et al. [35] discovered that microbial diversity was positively affected 
by the oxygen. As shown in Fig. 7a, the top 4 dominant phyla for MA0 
and MA0.2 were Bacteroidota, Firmicutes, Synergistota and Spirochaetota 
in that order, while the top 4 dominant phyla for MA1.6 were Firmicutes, 
Bacteroidota, Synergistota and Spirochaetota in that order. Bacteroidota 
was reported to possess the ability to decompose cellulose into cello­
biose and glucose and Firmicutes could secrete extracellular hydrolytic 
enzymes (e.g., cellulase, lipase and protease), thus accelerating the 
degradation of large molecules such as cellulose, protein and lipids 
[42,43]. The increased relative abundance of Firmicutes from MA0 to 
MA1.6 indicated the improved abilities of extracellular enzymes pro­
duction under micro-aeration conditions. Synergistota, also named Syn­
ergistetes, can produce short chain fatty acids and act as syntrophic 
acetate oxidizers [44]. Spirochaetota was a kind of acidogenic bacterium 
that could convert carbohydrates into simple VFAs [45]. The relative 
abundance of Spirochaetota of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 accounted for 
1.20%, 2.80% and 5.60%, respectively, which was in agreement with 
the reported results, i.e., 0.14–5.91% in the AD system with corn straw 
as the substrate [46]. The substantial increase of Spirochaetota from MA0 
to MA1.6 suggested the promotion of the acidification process by micro- 
aeration. The relative abundance of Firmicutes, Synergistota and

Spirochaetota of MA0.2 were 32.56%, 77.14% and 133.33% higher than 
that of MA0, respectively. The relative abundance of these three phyla of 
MA1.6 were 50.19%, 91.42% and 366.67% higher than that of MA0, 
respectively. These findings indicated the enhanced ability of AD to 
metabolize complex organics into small and simple molecules under 
micro-aeration conditions. 
Bacterial community structures of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 at family 
level are shown in Fig. 7b. The relative abundance of Lachnospiraceae 
affiliating with phylum Firmicutes was 7.49% in MA0.2 and 8.14% in 
MA1.6, which were 117.68% and 181.32% higher than that in MA0, 
respectively. Lachnospiraceae was responsible for the degradation of 
lignocellulose with high hydrolysis efficiency [47,48]. The increasing 
relative abundance of family Lachnospiraceae from MA0 to MA1.6 
demonstrated the increasing ability to break large cellulosic molecules 
of substrates into fermentable sugars under micro-aeration conditions. 
Spirochaetaceae (affiliating with phylum Spirochaetota) and Synergista­
ceae (affiliating with phylum Synergistota) were two well-known acetate- 
oxidizing bacteria, which were capable of oxidizing acetate into H2 and 
CO2 [49]. The relative abundance of Spirochaetaceae of MA0.2 and 
MA1.6 were 2.76% and 5.54%, which were 188.85% and 420.21% 
higher than that in MA0, respectively. Similarly, the relative abundance 
of Synergistaceae of MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 6.24% and 6.71%, which 
were 147.10% and 174.40% higher than that in MA0, respectively. 
Under micro-aerobic condition, the increase of the relative abundance of 
fermentative bacteria with the increase oxygen dose reflected the higher 
ability of AD to utilize the hydrolysis products from cellulosic biomass 
for producing VFAs. 
The hydrolysis of cellulosic substrate, such as corn straw has been 
recognized as the rate-limiting step during AD [50]. Therefore, 
compared to MA0, the increase of the relative abundances of the hy­
drolysis and fermentative bacteria in MA0.2 and MA1.6 under micro- 
aeration condition could in turn lead to higher hydrolysis and fermen­
tation rates. 
The Shannon diversity indexes of archaea increased slightly in 
MA0.2, but decreased rapidly in MA1.6, compared with MA0 (Fig. S4), 
which indicated that the archaeal diversity was negatively affected by 
oxygen. The reason behind this result might be that archaea especially 
methanogens are obligate anaerobic microbiota and the occurrence of 
oxygen could inhibit the growth of archaeal community in AD. As shown 
in Fig. 8, the dominant methanogens at genus level in MA0, MA0.2 and 
MA1.6 were Methanobacterium, Methanosarcina and Methanosaeta. 
However, the OTU reads and relative abundance of the genera varied 
with the increase of oxygen. According to Fig. 8a, the OTU reads of 
Methanobacterium, Methanosarcina and Methanosaeta of MA0.2 were 
1.32, 1.42 and 6.76 times of those of MA0 and the OTU reads of Meth­
anobacterium, Methanosarcina and Methanosaeta of MA1.6 were 1.46, 
0.12 and 9.06 times of those of MA0. Methanobacterium and Meth­
anosarcina were dominant genera in both MA0 and MA0.2, while the 
dominant genera were only Methanobacterium (the relative abundance 
was 84.05% and 1.73 times of that of MA0) of MA1.6. All the three 
dominant archaeal genera can survive and even grow better in the 
presence of limited amount of oxygen. Nevertheless, the OTU reads of 
Methanobacterium and Methanosaeta continued to show better adaption 
even under high oxygen concentration (i.e., MA1.6), whereas the OTU 
reads of Methanosarcina decreased rapidly. The above-mentioned results 
indicated that the archaeal community compositions changed with 
micro-aerobic condition and the oxygen tolerance of Methanosarcina was 
lower than that of Methanobacterium and Methanosaeta. 
4. Discussion 
Using micro-aeration to regulate the microbial community has

attracted increasing attention due to its potential economic and envi­
ronmental benefits. However, the underlying mechanisms of how micro- 
aeration benefit the AD process are largely unrevealed. In current study, 
the effects of micro-aeration on AD of corn straw were investigated. In 
order to figure out how micro-aeration benefits the AD process, 
comprehensively analytic methods including intermediate products 
analysis, model-based analysis, microbial community structure analysis, 
cyclic voltammetry (CV) and conductivity tests were conducted. Based 
on these experimental results, the mechanisms behind the benefits of 
micro-aeration were proposed and illustrated in Fig. 9. The oxygen 
introduced into the AD reactor could stimulate the growth of facultative 
microbes (e.g., phylum Firmicutes in Fig. 7) that in turn produced more 
extracellular enzymes (e.g., cellulase) [47,48] and enhanced the hy­
drolysis of corn straw. This inference could be confirmed by the higher 
VFAs and SHAs concentrations and higher removal rate of polymeric 
components of corn straw (i.e., cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin). 
Furthermore, Spirochaetaceae (phylum Spirochaetota in Fig. 7b) and 
Synergistaceae (phylum Synergistota in Fig. 7b) were equipped with the 
ability to oxidize acetate into H2 and CO2 and provide substrates (i.e., H2 
and CO2) for methanogenesis [49], which were also stimulated by 
micro-aeration. The hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis was proposed as 
a preferable methane production pathway in AD reactors operated in 
micro-aerobic conditions [11]. The increasing VFAs concentrations 
(Fig. 3A) and relative abundance of Synergistota and Spirochaetota (ac­
etate-oxidizing bacteria) (Fig. 7) under micro-aerobic condition sug­
gested more substrate CO2 and H2 for the faster metabolisms of 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens. 
In addition to the variation of bacterial communities, some archaea 
also acclimatized themselves to the micro-aeration condition. Meth­
anobacterium, Methanosaeta and Methanosarcina were reported to be able 
to survive even grow better in the presence of a small amount of oxygen 
[41]. Generally, these three archaea belong to hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens, acetoclastic methanogens and versatile methanogens 
(capable of utilizing acetate, methylamines, methanol and H2 /CO2), 
respectively [51–53]. The archaeal diversities decreased in the presence 
of excess oxygen, while the oxygen-tolerant methanogens (e.g., Meth­
anobacterium) became dominant and ensured the methanogenesis to 
produce methane. 
Apart from the microbial community variations, here we firstly 
found the enhanced DIET based syntrophic methane production under 
micro-aeration could be another non-negligible factor. Microbial meta­
bolism could convert some corn straw components into SHAs, which 
could serve as electron shutters and act as mediators for DIET [54–56]. 
The final concentrations of SHAs of MA0, MA0.2 and MA1.6 were 1.31 
± 0.06 g/L, 1.67 ± 0.12 g/L and 2.05 ± 0.10 g/L, respectively (Fig. 4). 
The higher SHAs under micro-aerobic condition appeared to empower 
the AD system with higher capacity of electron transfer (proved by the 
FTIR analysis results, Fig. S2 and CV experiment, Fig. 5a) and better 
conductive environment (proved by conductivity testing results, Fig. 5b) 
for syntrophic microorganisms, which indicated their stronger ability of 
DIET. Meanwhile, the relative abundances of organics-oxidizing bacte­
ria, acetate-oxidizing bacteria ((e.g., Spirochaetaceae and Synergistaceae 
(Fig. 7)) and methanogenic archaea ((e.g., Methanobacterium, Meth­
anosarcina and Methanosaeta (Fig. 8)) that associate with DIET also 
increased, which reflected the enhanced DIET under micro-aeration 
condition. 
These aforementioned factors were considered to work together to 
improve methane yield under micro-aeration condition. However, the 
micro-aeration intensity over 0.2 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day) decreased cumulative 
methane yield (Fig. 1). Such a decrease under excess micro-aeration 
intensity could be explained by: 1) The excess nonproductive con­
sumption of available substrates. The introduced oxygen could stimulate 
the growth of facultative microbes that could consume part of the sub­
strates without producing methane, i.e., the substrates towards methane 
production were reduced; and 2) The inhibition of methanogens by 
oxygen. Although some methanogens, such as Methanobacterium, 
Methanosarcina and Methanosaeta have a certain of oxygen tolerance, 
their tolerance is limited. Therefore, overdose of oxygen during micro- 
aeration could result in an inhibition to these methanogens. Similarly, 
Yu et al. [13] also found a reduction of methane production in the AD 
reactor at high oxygen dose (50 and 150 mg O2/L-reactor/cycle) when 
studying the effects of micro-aeration on the performance of AD of 
black-water. 
5. Conclusions 
This study evaluated the effects of micro-aeration on AD of corn 
straw. Micro-aeration could be conducive to the AD process depending 
on the oxygen dosage. Appropriate micro-aeration shortened the lag- 
phase and enhanced the methane yield, while excessive micro- 
aeration reduced the methane yield. Under proper micro-aeration, the 
relative abundances of facultative bacteria and oxygen-tolerant metha­
nogens were increased, meanwhile the DIET during AD was also 
enhanced, thus improving the methane yield. However, excess micro- 
aeration increased the nonproductive consumption of available sub­
strates (originally for methane production) while resulting in the inhi­
bition of methanogens, which lowered the methane yield. This study 
shows micro-aeration is a promising approach to improve the methane 
production of AD. However, the micro-aeration intensity should be well 
controlled.
